[IBNKATHIR:111:1/r1] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir identifies Sūrat al-Masad as a Meccan sūra.

[IBNKATHIR:111:1/r11] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | The second phrase confirms that Abu Lahab's ruin and destruction have indeed occurred.
[IBNKATHIR:111:1/r2] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | In the Bukhari report from Ibn Abbas, the Prophet calls Quraysh to gather at al-Batha, asks whether they would believe a warning of an imminent enemy, and warns of severe punishment; Abu Lahab objects that this was why they were gathered, curses the Prophet, and the sūra is revealed.
[IBNKATHIR:111:1/r3] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ابن عباس | reports | An alternate wording has Abu Lahab shake dust from his hands and say, 'Perish you all day; was this why you gathered us?' before the revelation.

[IBNKATHIR:111:1/r5] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Abu Lahab was the Prophet's paternal uncle, Abd al-Uzza ibn Abd al-Muttalib, also known by the kunya Abu Utba; he was nicknamed Abu Lahab for his shining face.
[IBNKATHIR:111:1/r6] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir says Abu Lahab repeatedly harmed the Messenger, hated and scorned him, and belittled him and his religion.
[IBNKATHIR:111:1/r7] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · ربيعة بن عباد الديلي | reports | Rabi'a ibn Abbad recalls seeing the Prophet preach that affirming God's oneness brings success in the market of Dhu al-Majaz, while Abu Lahab followed him calling him a lying Sabi. [IBNKATHIR:111:1/r8] IBNKATHIR, d. 774 · author | holds | Ibn Kathir notes that Ahmad alone transmits this account; Rabi'a says he was not a child then, since he could already carry a waterskin.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p514#2/r1] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ابن عباس عن النبي صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet warned Quraysh from Mount Safa that a severe punishment was coming; Abu Lahab cursed him, and the chapter was revealed.

[IBNKATHIR-FULL:v8p514#2/r4] IBNKATHIR-FULL, d. 774 · ربيعة بن عباد الديلي | reports | Rabi'a recalls seeing the Prophet call people to profess God's oneness at the market of Dhu al-Majaz while his uncle followed, calling him a lying Sabian.

[BURHAN:v1p438/r2] BURHAN, d. 794 · مالك | reports | Malik’s view is reported as denying preference; Yahya ibn Yahya calls it wrong to prefer one part, and Malik disliked repeatedly reciting one surah over others.
[BURHAN:v1p438/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | prefers | Al-Zarkashi prefers that preference rests on the abundance and wonder of meanings: divine unity and attributes occur in these passages but not in the curse on Abu Lahab.

[BURHAN:v1p439/r6] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي شمس الدين الخويي | reports | Al-Khuyi says eloquence comparisons must respect each passage’s purpose: no wording better invokes ruin than Tabbat, and no wording better states divine unity than al-Ikhlas, so neither is absolutely more eloquent.
[BURHAN:v1p439/r7] BURHAN, d. 794 · القاضي شمس الدين الخويي | reports | Comparing al-Ikhlas directly with Tabbat is misguided if it pits divine mention against Abu Lahab or monotheism against a curse; each is most eloquent in its own subject.
[BURHAN:v2p114/r9] BURHAN, d. 794 · author | reports | The author adds Qur’anic phrases as examples of metrical coincidence, including night worship, charity, disputing, the flood, Abu Lahab, victory, conversion, and Qarun. | mentions 50:40, 3:92, 18:22, 11:43, 111:1, 61:13, 8:38, 28:76

[NASHR:v2p203/r5] NASHR, d. 833 · محمد بن بضحان | reports | The teacher Muḥammad ibn Baḍḥān rebuked a man who stopped after “the hands of Abū Lahab” and repeated it to demonstrate all the madd lengths.
[NASHR:v2p404/r10] NASHR, d. 833 · أبو شامة | prefers | Abu Shama explains Ibn Kathir’s sukūn as easing a name heavy on the tongue because its referent weighs on the heart; Ibn al-Jazari praises this explanation.
[NASHR:v2p404/r8] NASHR, d. 833 · ابن كثير، الباقون | reports | Ibn Kathir reads the hāʾ in Abu Lahab with sukūn; the other readers give it fatḥ.

[BIQAI:111:1/r18] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The closing clause makes explicit that the ruin concerns Abū Lahab himself in his entirety, not merely literal loss of his hands.
[BIQAI:111:1/r19] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | prefers | The apparent construction is a curse or prayer in the first clause followed by a factual report in the second.
[BIQAI:111:1/r2] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Abū Lahab was the Prophet's close relative and a notorious, intensely hostile tormentor of him and his leadership.
[BIQAI:111:1/r20] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The clarification confirms the hand-expression as a figure for utter destruction, leaving no life or recovery afterward.
[BIQAI:111:1/r21] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Being related to a righteous person does not avail without following that person's deeds; Abū Lahab was the Prophet's uncle.
[BIQAI:111:1/r22] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The roots tabb and batt center on severance that commonly leads to ruin: severing oneself from the ultimate Cause for lesser means brings loss, and exhausting all means can still frustrate one's aims.
[BIQAI:111:1/r23] BIQAI, d. 885 · ابن مكتوم | reports | Ibn Maktūm's lexicon defines tabb and tibāb as loss, and tabban lahu as a curse; tabban tabīban intensifies it.
[BIQAI:111:1/r24] BIQAI, d. 885 · القزاز | reports | Al-Qazzāz parses tabban lahu as a verbal noun meaning ‘loss to him,’ accusative like suqyan lahu.
[BIQAI:111:1/r25] BIQAI, d. 885 · ابن دريد | reports | Ibn Durayd distinguishes tabb as a verbal noun from tibāb as a noun; tabab, tibāb, and tabīb mean ruin, while tatbīb means deficiency and loss.
[BIQAI:111:1/r26] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Other lexical senses extend the root to an old man or woman, a weak person, and a donkey or camel with a damaged back, all suggesting decline toward severance or death.
[BIQAI:111:1/r27] BIQAI, d. 885 · القزاز | reports | Al-Qazzāz explains tabba as an old, failing woman, a sense linked to age's nearness to severance and death.
[BIQAI:111:1/r28] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Tabba can mean ‘cut’ like batt; falling into tabūb or being in tabba describes a dire condition; tibbi is a low-grade Bahrain date eaten by common people.
[BIQAI:111:1/r29] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Derived forms mean weakening someone's strength, destroying them, or growing old, continuing the root's sense of decline and ruin.
[BIQAI:111:1/r3] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The sūra's placement after victory recalls the early persecution and proves that the disbelievers' numbers, arms, alliances, and pacts could not defeat God's promise in 3:12. | mentions 3:12
[BIQAI:111:1/r30] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Tubūb can denote the chest or heart enclosed by the ribs; this may be read positively or negatively because a sound or corrupt heart affects the whole body.
[BIQAI:111:1/r31] BIQAI, d. 885 · القزاز | reports | Al-Qazzāz says istatabba means that a matter became prepared and settled; he also notes that a proposed analogy does not hold in comparable expressions.
[BIQAI:111:1/r32] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The author associates the sīn in istatabba with completion, interpreting it as bringing the matter fully to success and clarity.
[BIQAI:111:1/r33] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The reversed root batt makes explicit the stronger, outward severance that depends on a complete inward cause.
[BIQAI:111:1/r34] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Batt and abatta mean to cut something completely; alignment across basic, derived, intransitive, and transitive forms suggests the cutting is already maximal.
[BIQAI:111:1/r35] BIQAI, d. 885 · سيبويه | reports | Sībawayh says qaʿada al-battata is an emphatic verbal noun construction, used only with the definite article.
[BIQAI:111:1/r36] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The root appears in definitive truth, irrevocable triple divorce, and al-battata (‘never’), figuratively severing doubt, return, or an intended act.
[BIQAI:111:1/r37] BIQAI, d. 885 · القزاز | reports | Al-Qazzāz distinguishes yubittu from abatta and yabittu from batta; batt describes incoherent drunken speech, and a batt drunkard is cut off from work.
[BIQAI:111:1/r38] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Abatta can mean to carry through an oath, while battat can mean that something became established or due; both derive from severance.
[BIQAI:111:1/r39] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | reports | A hadith calls the person who exhausts his mount until its back fails al-munbat, leaving him stranded; al-Qazzāz gives the same explanation.
[BIQAI:111:1/r4] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Choosing the Prophet's nearest enemy signals that kin and stranger are equally subject to God's judgment; kinship did not help Abū Lahab.
[BIQAI:111:1/r40] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The root also describes fixing or imposing testimony and judgment; a bat is an emaciated person too weak to stand, as though his strength were cut off.
[BIQAI:111:1/r41] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | reports | A hadith's phrase ‘no fast for one who did not yubit fasting at night’ means resolving and obligating the fast before dawn; yubit from batta is another eloquent form with the same meaning, and a version uses yabit from bayāt.
[BIQAI:111:1/r42] BIQAI, d. 885 · الليث | reports | Al-Layth defines ahmaq batt as extreme foolishness; al-Azharī instead says the word is tabb, with bāʾ delayed.
[BIQAI:111:1/r43] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-batt is a coarse, loose, square green cloak, said to be made of camel hair and wool; its plural is butūt.
[BIQAI:111:1/r44] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Al-battāt means household belongings or travel provisions, either because they cut off need or because they remove deprivation by supplying and helping the owner.
[BIQAI:111:1/r45] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The author proposes that each root family has a dominant sense and forms that remove or reverse it; assistance and provision exemplify such removal.
[BIQAI:111:1/r46] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Being ʿalā battat amr means nearing completion, when the matter is about to end.
[BIQAI:111:1/r47] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Grinding with the mill turning leftward marks fully resolved purpose because it gives the grinder greater strength and control.
[BIQAI:111:1/r48] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Inbatt can mean a man's semen was depleted; a single-strand cord is called batt because it is easily cut, and inbatta ʿan someone means he withdrew and severed contact.
[BIQAI:111:1/r5] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The past tense presents the ruin as already decreed, complete, inevitable, and inescapable.
[BIQAI:111:1/r6] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Tabbat conveys the greatest severance and definitive loss, ending in destruction, since only salvation in the afterlife is true salvation.
[BIQAI:111:1/r7] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Unlike sister sūras introduced by qul, this sūra speaks directly in God's voice: the form is more decorous toward kin, stronger in God's vindication of the Prophet, and more immediately alarming.
[BIQAI:111:1/r8] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | Because hands are the seat of human capacity, naming both signifies that all Abū Lahab's power failed; the dual can also stand for the whole person.
[BIQAI:111:1/r9] BIQAI, d. 885 · author | holds | The kunya, though often honorific, fits Abū Lahab's condition and makes clear that he could neither give nor withhold, help nor harm.
